payload.rationale: I estimate a 4% chance that September’s published, seasonally adjusted U-3 rate is strictly above 4.4%, meaning at least 4.5% at the reported one-decimal precision. The supplied BLS evidence reports 4.1% in both July and August, following 4.2% in June. YES therefore requires a rise of at least 0.4 percentage points in the published rate in one month—an unusually large move under ordinary labor-market conditions. August payroll growth of 162,000 also weighs against an abrupt deterioration, although payroll employment and household-survey unemployment are different measures. This is a judgmental tail probability, not a statistically fitted estimate. The strongest reason it could be too high is that stable recent unemployment and continued payroll growth may make such a jump even less likely. The strongest reason it could be too low is that June and July payroll gains were revised to only 31,000 and 21,000, potentially indicating underlying weakness; household-survey variability or a participation increase could also lift unemployment unexpectedly.
limitations: Only three recent unemployment readings are supplied; they do not establish a calibrated distribution of monthly changes.
September survey results and other relevant current labor-market indicators are unavailable. Supplied release claims cannot be independently verified here.

The listed event deadline is 12:29 UTC on October 2, one minute before the supplied scheduled release time. I interpret YES as the stated September BLS outcome; any separate deadline-based settlement treatment is unclear from the supplied rules.
